directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun so roots establish before the dry season. Puget Blue is a dense, mounding evergreen selected at the UC Santa Cruz Arboretum, prized for its deep indigo-blue flower clusters in mid to late spring and for tolerating heavier soils better than many ceanothus. Avoid summer irrigation once established and avoid heavy phosphorus fertilizer, both of which shorten the shrub's naturally short lifespan. Prune lightly right after bloom to keep the habit dense, since ceanothus does not resprout reliably from old wood.
sources: UC Santa Cruz Arboretum and Botanic Garden

common_name: Diamond Heights Ceanothus (Variegated Groundcover California Lilac)
directions: Plant this low, spreading sport of Carmel creeper in fall in well-drained soil, giving it filtered sun or partial shade rather than the blazing full sun that other ceanothus tolerate, since strong sun can scorch the bright yellow-and-green variegated foliage. Diamond Heights is grown primarily as a foliage groundcover; its pale blue flowers in spring are a secondary feature. Keep irrigation minimal once roots are established and avoid soggy, poorly drained sites, which quickly cause root rot in this genus.

Plant this naturally occurring low, spreading form of blueblossom in fall along banks or as a wide-spreading groundcover, in full sun near the coast or light afternoon shade further inland. It produces the same abundant powder-blue to medium-blue flower clusters as the upright species in spring but stays low and mounding, making it useful for erosion control on slopes. Give it excellent drainage and withhold summer water once established; it is highly drought-adapted but short-lived in heavy clay or irrigated turf-adjacent beds.

Plant container-grown shrubs in fall into lean, sharply drained, low-fertility soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since flannel bush resents root disturbance and transplants poorly once established. California Glory is a long-blooming, mostly evergreen hybrid selection valued for its extended late-spring-through-summer display of large golden-yellow flowers and for tolerating garden conditions better than the wild species. Never irrigate it during summer once established and never amend the planting hole with rich soil, both of which encourage root and crown rot. Wear gloves and eye protection when pruning, since the fine hairs covering the stems and seed capsules are a significant skin and eye irritant.

Plant in a warm, sheltered, full-sun position with sharply drained, lean soil, reserving this species for the mildest gardens since it is markedly more frost-tender than the more widely grown Fremontodendron californicum. Native to a few sites in San Diego County and northern Baja California, it bears larger leaves and larger golden-yellow flowers than its northern relative, opening from late winter into summer. Withhold summer water entirely once the plant is established, and avoid disturbing the root zone; like other flannel bushes it resents transplanting and rich or poorly drained soils promote root rot. Handle with gloves, since the stellate hairs covering stems and fruit readily irritate skin and eyes.

Plant container-grown or bare-root stock in fall in lean, rocky or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; birchleaf mountain mahogany is a common chaparral and foothill-woodland shrub throughout California and the desert Southwest and thrives on neglect once roots are established. Its small, rounded, birch-like leaves are semi-evergreen to deciduous depending on climate, and the shrub is grown mainly for wildlife cover and its distinctive twisted, silvery-plumed seed tails rather than showy flowers. It tolerates poor, rocky soils that few other landscape shrubs will grow in and needs no supplemental water once mature, but resents heavy or frequently irrigated soils.

Plant in rocky, alkaline, extremely well-drained soil in full sun on the driest, most exposed part of the landscape; littleleaf mountain mahogany is one of the slowest-growing and longest-lived shrubs of the Colorado Plateau and Great Basin, forming dense, gnarled, tangled evergreen thickets over many decades. Its tiny, needle-like, rolled-margin leaves are an extreme adaptation to aridity, allowing it to persist on exposed slickrock and mesa edges with essentially no irrigation. Because of its slow growth, start with the largest container stock available and expect minimal size increase for the first several years; established plants need no supplemental water and resist browsing better than most desert shrubs.

Plant container-grown stock in fall into lean, fast-draining soil, giving it light afternoon shade in hot inland gardens or full coastal sun. Emerald Carpet is a dense, low, mounding hybrid manzanita grown mainly for its glossy, bright green evergreen foliage, small pinkish-white urn-shaped flowers in late winter, and reliable performance as a durable groundcover under oaks and other natives. Water occasionally during the first year or two to establish a deep root system, then taper off, since overwatering established plants is the most common cause of failure in this genus. Avoid summer overhead irrigation and heavy or poorly drained soils to prevent branch dieback and root rot.

Plant nursery-grown plugs or container stock in fall into sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Massachusetts is the most widely sold bearberry cultivar in the nursery trade, selected for a dense, compact, fast-spreading habit, small glossy leaves that turn bronze-red in winter, and good resistance to leaf spot compared with the straight species. It roots readily where trailing stems touch soil, forming a tight evergreen mat useful for erosion control on sandy or rocky slopes. Keep new plantings watered through the first season, then reduce irrigation, since established plants are highly drought tolerant and intolerant of wet, poorly drained soils.

Plant container-grown stock in fall into lean, rocky, sharply drained soil in full sun, siting it as a small multi-trunked specimen tree since Dr. Hurd matures into one of the largest and most tree-like of the cultivated manzanitas. It is prized for smooth, deep mahogany-red bark, an open branching structure, clean gray-green foliage, and abundant clusters of small white to pale pink urn-shaped flowers in late winter that draw hummingbirds. Give it excellent drainage and no summer irrigation once established, since wet feet during the dormant or growing season quickly leads to fatal root and crown rot in this genus. Prune only to reveal the branching structure, never into old wood.

Plant container-grown stock in fall into lean, sandy or rocky, well-drained soil in full coastal sun or light inland shade. Carmel Sur is a low, dense, mat-forming selection of the Santa Lucia Mountains native Little Sur manzanita, valued as a durable evergreen groundcover with small gray-green leaves and pink-tinged white flowers in winter followed by small red berries. It tolerates coastal wind and salt exposure well and spreads steadily without becoming aggressive, making it a good bank or slope cover near the coast. Keep it on the dry side once established, since summer irrigation and heavy soils are the most common causes of decline in cultivated manzanitas.

Plant container-grown shrubs or root hardwood cuttings in fall in moist but well-drained, adaptable soil in full sun near the coast or partial shade inland. King Edward VII is a compact, long-popular selection of the Pacific Northwest native red-flowering currant, chosen for its unusually deep crimson-red flower clusters that open in early to mid spring before the leaves fully expand, drawing hummingbirds just as they return north. Its more restrained size compared with the species makes it well suited to smaller borders and foundation plantings. Water during the first year or two to establish, then reduce, since mature plants tolerate considerable summer drought but appreciate occasional deep watering in hot inland climates.

Plant container-grown shrubs or root hardwood cuttings in fall in moist but well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. White Icicle is a white-flowered sport of the Pacific Northwest native red-flowering currant, opening pendant clusters of pure white flowers in early spring against fresh green, lobed foliage, and it makes a good companion to pink- and red-flowered forms in a mixed native border. It shares the species' drought tolerance once established but performs best with occasional deep watering during hot, dry summers. Prune out a portion of the oldest stems right after flowering to keep the shrub vigorous and well shaped.

Plant container-grown shrubs or root hardwood cuttings in fall in moist but well-drained, adaptable soil in full sun to partial shade. Pulborough Scarlet, a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit holder, bears dark red flower clusters with distinctive pale-centered petals in early to mid spring on a somewhat larger, more vigorous frame than many other named selections. Give it room to reach its mature size and avoid crowding, since good air circulation reduces the powdery mildew this genus can develop in humid, still conditions. It tolerates considerable summer drought once established but flowers and grows best with occasional deep watering in hot inland gardens.
